blocks.text: After the greeting, the chapter unfolds as an extended blessing. It gathers election, adoption, redemption, forgiveness, inheritance, the Spirit’s seal, and the summing up of all things in Christ into one account of what God has done and purposes to do. The prayer in verses 15–23 then asks that its readers grasp the hope, inheritance, and power described in that blessing.

The words translated “in Ephesus” in verse 1 are absent from some early Greek witnesses, although later transmission and title traditions associate the letter with Ephesus. This leaves the original destination uncertain: it cannot establish with certainty whether the letter was addressed solely to Ephesus, circulated more widely, or first heard in one particular house church. The letter speaks in a canonical Pauline voice, but direct Pauline authorship remains disputed.

The chapter’s language of choosing and foreordination is substantial, but it should not be turned into fatalism, despair, superiority, or a claim that people who suffer have been rejected by God. Likewise, the language of Christ as head over all things and of the church as his body has disputed referents; it does not authorize unaccountable human hierarchy. The vision of all things being summed up in Christ also resists treating human salvation as permission to neglect the nonhuman world.

Because the original destination remains uncertain, material from Ephesus should be treated as possible reception context rather than certain evidence about the letter’s first hearers. That caution also prevents the chapter’s imagery from being reduced to one local setting or civic concern.

Ephesians shares extensive language and structure with Colossians. The direction and mechanism of that relationship remain debated, so the resemblance is clear while explanations of how it arose are not settled.
